places_and_people.name: Kabul radio station
places_and_people.note: Radio Afghanistan began broadcasting in the 1950s and built the radio orchestra that created Afghan popular music.

places_and_people.name: Afghan court in Kabul
places_and_people.note: Musicians from India came to play at the Afghan court in Kabul in the 1860s. Their descendants are the Kabuli ustads of Klasik.

places_and_people.name: Pashtun people
places_and_people.note: The largest group, in the south and east. Their music is dramatic and rhythmic, and Pashto singing, including landai, belongs to wedding and folk practice.

places_and_people.name: Jat people
places_and_people.note: Specialists who make and sell the daireh. The men play the outdoor shawm-and-drum duo.

places_and_people.name: Sazdohol musicians
places_and_people.note: A shawm and double-headed dohol duo with semi-outcast status. They play for weddings, circumcisions, stick dances, and circle dances.

places_and_people.name: Bozkashi games
places_and_people.note: A northern winter horseback game. Sazdohol musicians play at it.

places_and_people.name: Melehs
places_and_people.note: Outdoor New Year fairs at the spring equinox, a main season for public music.

places_and_people.name: Mazar-i Sharif
places_and_people.note: The northern shrine. Its forty-day tulip festival has roots in pre-Islamic practice, and people play and listen outdoors there.

places_and_people.name: Tea-houses
places_and_people.note: Male rooms, especially in the north, where musicians sit on a bench and sing epics or popular songs with tanbur or ghichak.
